questiontext.text: Your capstone/aws root keeps its state in S3. Which backend setting makes two runs unable to change the state at the same time, without a DynamoDB table?

answer.text: use_lockfile = true
dynamodb_table = "tf-locks" — the S3 backend needs it for locking
encrypt = true — it encrypts the state and locks it during a run
Versioning on the state bucket — each run writes a new version, so runs can't overwrite each other

name.text: TF02 — Where the Generated Password Lives

questiontext.text:
The rds-mysql module generates the database password with random_password and stores it in Secrets Manager. terraform plan shows it only as (sensitive value).

Where else does the password exist, and why does that matter?

answer.text: In the Terraform state (the random_password result), which is why the state bucket must be encrypted and private
Nowhere else: a value marked sensitive is never written to state
Only in Secrets Manager: Terraform discards the value once the secret version is created
In .terraform.lock.hcl, which is why the lock file must never be committed

name.text: TF03 — Replies Without an Egress Rule

questiontext.text: In the capstone, the DB security group has one ingress rule (3306 from the App group) and zero egress rules. Yet the Flashcard API still gets its query results back from MySQL. Why?

answer.text: Security groups are stateful: replies to an allowed inbound connection are allowed back automatically
Terraform keeps AWS's default allow-all egress rule on every new security group
The DB route table has a route back to the App subnets, and routes override security groups
The replies travel through the S3 gateway endpoint attached to the DB route table

name.text: TF04 — Attaching a New Parameter Group

questiontext.text:
You attach a new parameter group to the running RDS instance:

parameter {
  name         = "slow_query_log"
  value        = "1"
  apply_method = "immediate"
}

The plan says aws_db_instance.this will be updated in-place, and the apply succeeds. Is the slow-query log on now?

answer.text: Not yet: a newly attached group applies, even its dynamic parameters, only after one reboot (status pending-reboot)
Yes: slow_query_log is dynamic and apply_method is "immediate", so it takes effect with no reboot
No: attaching a parameter group replaces the DB instance, so it's on only after the new instance is created
No: with create_before_destroy the group only becomes active on the next terraform apply

name.text: TF05 — Removing the First Item: count vs for_each

questiontext.text:
Three instances are built from a list with count:

names = ["web-a", "web-b", "web-c"]   # removing "web-a"

What does the next plan do, compared with building them with for_each over a map keyed by name?

answer.text: With count, the later indexes shift: [0] and [1] change or are replaced, and [2] is destroyed. With for_each, only "web-a" is destroyed
Both behave the same: only the instance named "web-a" is destroyed
With count, only [0] is destroyed; with for_each, all three are replaced because the map changed
Neither changes anything until you run terraform state rm on the removed item

name.text: TF06 — Planning in the Wrong Workspace

questiontext.text:
You forget to select a workspace, so you're in default, and you run:

terraform plan -var-file=env/dev.tfvars

env/dev.tfvars sets environment = "dev". What happens?

answer.text: The plan fails at the workspace_guard preconditions: the default workspace is not used, and var.environment must match the workspace
The plan fails at variable validation, because "default" is not one of dev, staging or prod
The plan succeeds and would create resources named tf-bootcamp-default-*
terraform init fails, because the S3 backend has no state file for the default workspace

name.text: TF07 — Switching Off the NAT Gateway Mid-Capstone

questiontext.text:
The full dev stack is applied (App ASG minimum = 1). To save money you run:

terraform plan -var-file=env/dev.tfvars -var nat_gateway_enabled=false

The root contains this guard:

resource "terraform_data" "nat_guard" {
  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = var.nat_gateway_enabled || local.size.app_min == 0
      error_message = "App instances need the NAT Gateway. Set nat_gateway_enabled = true."
    }
  }
}

What does the plan do?

answer.text: It fails with "App instances need the NAT Gateway", so nothing is planned
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy (the NAT Gateway, its EIP and the App route), as in the M4 lab
It destroys the NAT, and the App servers reach the internet through the S3 gateway endpoint instead
It moves the App Auto Scaling group into the public subnets so the servers keep internet access

questiontext.text: Your M10 apply has just finished. You open web_url: the Flashcard Quiz page loads, and /api/health returns {"status":"ok"}, but the page says "Cards unavailable … Is the database up?". What's the right move?

answer.text: Wait and reload: RDS is the slowest resource, and the API connects as soon as the DB endpoint appears in SSM
Start an instance refresh on the App ASG: the API gave up waiting for the database after 20 minutes
Open port 3306 on the Web security group, because the page calls the database from the browser
Add secretsmanager:GetSecretValue with resource "*" to the instance role so the API can read any secret

name.text: TF09 — CORS With the Lookup Switched Off

questiontext.text: With the AWS stack up, you apply capstone/multicloud with -var lookup_web_alb=false, so the CORS rule's allowed origin falls back to http://localhost:8080. You reload the Flashcard Quiz from web_url. What does its footer say about the Azure assets?

answer.text: "Azure Blob ✗ (blocked by CORS)": the logo is loaded with fetch(), and Azure doesn't allow the Web ALB's origin
"Azure Blob ✓ (CORS allowed)": the container allows anonymous blob reads, so CORS doesn't apply
"built-in styles (Azure not connected yet)": the app ignores Azure whenever the lookup is off
Nothing: the whole page fails to load, because index.html is served from Azure

name.text: TF10 — Is the Account Really Clean?

questiontext.text: While debugging, you launched an EC2 instance by hand in the AWS console, in the account's default VPC. At the end of the session you run terraform destroy in both roots, and terraform state list prints nothing in either. Is your account clean?

answer.text: No: Terraform only tracks what it created. The hand-made instance was never in state, so it's still running and billing
Yes: terraform destroy removes every resource tagged Project = tf-bootcamp
Yes: the provider's default_tags adopt new resources into state on the next run
Yes: if anything were still running, the $5 budget alert would already have warned you
